subject: Private visibility: telemetry data-mesh handshake, ingress/egress and SIEM mapping
messages:
From: Acme Health Security <security@acmehealth.com>
To: marcus.lin@redwood.com
Cc: netops@acmehealth.com, splunk-admin@acmehealth.com
Date: 2027-05-30T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Request: private deploy observability — egress/ingest & field mapping

Marcus,

Thanks for agreeing to review our on-prem / VPC observability plan for the Redwood private deployment. Two priorities from our side: (1) we need a clear, auditable path for logs/traces/metrics out of our VPC to our Splunk instance (or a signed evidence bundle if we can't egress), and (2) PHI-aware field mapping / redaction rules that you support in the forwarder so we can stay within our retention and compliance policies.

Questions to start with:
- Do you require outbound internet egress from our VPC to a Redwood endpoint, or can the forwarder be run in our account and deliver directly to our Splunk HEC inside the VPC?
- For cases where we must move data off-network (Splunk Cloud), what encryption/mTLS and nat/proxy topology do you recommend?
- How do you propose proving delivery / chain-of-custody for audit (signed envelopes, sequence numbers, timestamps)?
- Can we push a pre-configured mapping file for field-level redaction and tokenization, or do we need a job on your side?

Attached: brief CSV with fields we care about and examples of what needs redaction.

We'd like a short architecture note + runbook we can hand to our NetOps team and the Splunk team. Can your team produce that by EOD tomorrow so we can schedule a 30-min handoff?

Thanks,
Dana Murphy
Information Security Manager
Acme Health

From: marcus.lin@redwood.com
To: security@acmehealth.com, splunk-admin@acmehealth.com
Cc: kimberly.park@redwood.com, marissa.cole@redwood.com
Date: 2027-05-30T10:04:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Request: private deploy observability — egress/ingest & field mapping

Dana — thanks for the clear ask. High level answers up front, followed by a proposed minimal-risk pattern and open questions.

High-level options (we'll produce a short runbook + network snippets):
1) In-account forwarder (recommended when customers disallow outbound egress):
   - Deploy Redwood forwarder sidecar(s) into a customer-managed private subnet. The forwarder writes directly to an internal Splunk HEC endpoint (private IP) or to an S3-compatible staging bucket in the customer's account.
   - Advantages: no egress, customers keep full control of keys and retention. Redwood's control plane is optional and can be run over a dedicated, customer-managed VPN if desired.

2) Controlled egress (when Splunk Cloud / external collector is required):
   - Forwarder aggregates -> mutual-TLS (mTLS) to Redwood egress gateway within a designated egress NAT pool. All connections use client certs issued per customer with short TTL and automated rotation.
   - We support batching (HEC compressed batches) with sequence numbers and signed JSON envelopes for proof-of-delivery. When customer requires, we can mirror the signed envelopes back into customer-owned encrypted storage for audits.

Redaction / mapping / trace considerations:
- Mapping: we can consume a CSV mapping file (column name, pii_level, redaction_type, keep_mask_pattern). We'll run the mapping as a local transformation in the forwarder (preferred) to avoid PHI leaving the VPC. See attached telemetry_field_map_v2.csv.
- Sampling & tracecorrelation: keep 100% traces for error spans; use deterministic sampling by tenant_id for perf spans. Propagate X-Redwood-Trace header and include hashed_device_id and tenant_id in span tags (sha256 truncated) for SIEM correlation without exposing raw PII.
- Chain of custody: every batch has sequence number, batch_ts, and a signed sha256 envelope. We keep a per-batch ack log for 90 days (extendable). Customers can opt-in to have those ack logs mirrored to a customer-owned encrypted S3.

Network & deployment notes (short):
- If in-account forwarder -> create a Splunk HEC internal LB, allow 10.0.2.0/24 (forwarder subnet) inbound on 8088 with mutual TLS.
- If egress -> route forwarder subnet to NAT Gateway / egress gateway with stateful firewall allowing outbound on 443 to Redwood egress pool IPs; use security groups + IP allowlist.

Next steps I propose:
- We produce a 1-page runbook + network snippets and an example mapping CSV by EOD today.
- NetOps review against your security policy; if OK, we schedule 30-min handoff with NetOps + Splunk team tomorrow.

Attaching: telemetry_field_map_v2.csv (mapping examples).

If any of the above constrains your audit path, call it out and we'll adapt (e.g., signed evidence bundle instead of egress).

—Marcus Lin
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
marcus.lin@redwood.com

From: kimberly.park@redwood.com

Date: 2027-05-30T12:31:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Request: private deploy observability — egress/ingest & field mapping

Looping in the runbook and some concrete network snippets for NetOps. I focused on the private-forwarder pattern and an egress-safe alternative.

Key excerpts from runbook (attached 'evidence-transfer-runbook.pdf'):
- Deployable artifacts: 1) forwarder Helm chart (daemonset in telemetry namespace), 2) optional ingress LB + internal HEC config, 3) policy CRD for mapping/redaction.
- TLS & auth: we require mTLS for all HEC endpoints. For in-account HEC, provide a CA bundle; for egress to Redwood, we'll use customer-bounded client certs (certs rotate via ACME-like flow; recommended 30d TTL).
- Network rules: example iptables / egress-proxy rule to ensure only TLS 443 to allowed IPs is permitted from forwarder host. Sample route table: forwarder-subnet -> (route) egress-proxy -> NAT-gateway -> Internet; alternate route: forwarder-subnet -> VPC endpoint -> splunk-internal-lb.
- Trace hooks: add two mandatory headers for all outgoing spans: X-Redwood-Trace (trace id), X-Redwood-Source (forwarder-id). Both should be logged in Splunk as indexed fields. Retain trace parent info for 7 days; full span payload kept per customer retention policy.
- Evidence bundle flow (when customer disallows egress): the forwarder packages daily gzipped bundles, signs them with per-customer key, places them into the customer's S3 bucket path /redwood/evidence/YYYYMMDD/*. The runbook shows how to generate and verify signatures.

Network snippet (example):
- Security group: allow inbound tcp/8088 from 10.0.2.0/24 (forwarder subnet) to splunk-internal-lb.
- Route table entries: 10.0.2.0/24 -> local; 0.0.0.0/0 -> nat-gw-03 (only for approved egress).

Open items for NetOps:
- Confirm whether NetOps prefers in-account HEC or mirrored evidence bundles.
- Confirm maximum allowed egress rate (we recommend bursting up to 50MB/s for peak indexing jobs).

I've attached the runbook and included a short checklist for on-call (what to watch for during first 72 hours).

Kimberly Park
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
kimberly.park@redwood.com

Team — this is exactly the level of detail we needed. NetOps prefers the in-account forwarder -> internal HEC path, with evidence bundles as fallback for quarterly audits. Two quick confirmations: (1) we want the signed evidence bundles mirrored into our S3 bucket with server-side encryption and limited KMS key access (we'll provide the KMS ARN), and (2) we require that the forwarder performs initial PII redaction in-line (so raw PHI never leaves the subnet).

Can Redwood confirm by EOD tomorrow that:
- the forwarder Helm chart has a policy CRD to load the supplied mapping CSV and enforce redaction at transform-time, and
- the evidence bundles are signed using per-customer key material and written to the customer S3 path with the signature alongside each bundle.

If you can confirm, we'll stand up a staging VPC and schedule the 30-min handoff for next Tuesday 10am PT.

Thanks,
Dana Murphy
Information Security Manager
Acme Health
